plan: Second-price auctions make truthful bidding weakly dominant for a risk-neutral bidder, regardless of others’ strategies. With no history to exploit and independent uniform values (0–49), bidding my true value maximizes expected profit and avoids overpaying. Raising slightly above 36 to beat a tie only converts an expected zero-surplus tie into a deterministic zero-surplus win, offering no expected gain, and risks losses against higher bids. Therefore, I will bid exactly my value ($36). If future rounds existed with behavioral patterns, I’d adapt, but here it’s optimal to be truthful.

[ This is a sealed-bid, second-price auction with independent private values uniformly distributed. In such auctions, bidding your true value is a weakly dominant strategy: it maximizes expected profit regardless of others’ strategies. Shading risks losing when winning would be profitable, and overbidding risks negative payoff if the second price exceeds value. With no informative history and only one round, no learning applies. Therefore, bid exactly my value ($32). If tied at the top, the random tie-break is acceptable because expected payoff remains nonnegative when bidding truthfully. ]

[ This is a 3-bidder, second-price sealed-bid auction with independent private values. In such auctions, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy: it maximizes expected profit regardless of others’ strategies. There’s only 1 round and no history to exploit, so no scope for behavioral adjustments. With value $42, bidding 42 ensures I win exactly when my value is highest and pay the second-highest bid, yielding nonnegative surplus. I will bid 42 to comply with the $0.1 increment rule. ]
